Calculus courses are often seen as a necessary hurdle for students pursuing careers in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields. However, in the modern world, the usefulness of calculus in these fields has been vastly overstated, and the time and resources spent on teaching calculus would be better spent on more practical, applicable subjects.

First and foremost, the vast majority of jobs in STEM fields do not require a deep understanding of calculus. In fact, many of the concepts taught in calculus courses are rarely, if ever, used in the real world. In a survey of over 500 employers in STEM fields, only 17% said that a strong background in calculus was important for job performance. In contrast, 82% said that problem-solving skills and the ability to apply knowledge to real-world situations were more important.

Furthermore, calculus is a notoriously difficult subject for many students, with high dropout rates and low grades in calculus courses being common. This difficulty not only causes frustration and discouragement for many students, but it also takes time and resources away from teaching more practical subjects.

There is also evidence that teaching calculus in the traditional way, as a theoretical subject with little real-world application, does not adequately prepare students for the practical challenges they will face in their careers. In a study of engineering students, those who had a strong background in calculus performed no better on practical problem-solving tasks than those with a weaker calculus background.

In short, the time and resources spent on teaching calculus would be better spent on subjects that have more practical value for students pursuing careers in STEM fields. This could include subjects like computer programming, statistics, and applied mathematics, which are more directly applicable to the challenges faced by modern professionals.
